---
title: "Set Up Your Computer"
---

The course is a GitHub repository: it holds the notebooks, the pages of this website, the data and the scorer. You make your own copy of this repository on GitHub, download your copy to your computer and work in it there. Each time you save your work to your copy on GitHub, you have a backup and a history of your work, and you can continue on another computer.

Your copy is private, so your answers to the exercises stay yours. It is also a snapshot: it keeps the course version you started with, and later changes to the course don't reach it (see [Updates](#updates)).

You need a free GitHub account and three tools:

- **Git**, which keeps track of the changes to your files and sends them to GitHub;
- **uv**, which installs the right Python version (3.13) and every package the course uses. You don't need to install Python yourself;
- **VS Code**, the editor in which you open and run the notebooks.

The setup takes about 30 minutes. Everything together needs about 3 GB of disk space: the course environment (about 0.7 GB on macOS, about 1.5 GB on Linux, where XGBoost also installs GPU libraries) and uv's download cache, which you can empty afterwards with `uv cache clean`.

::: {.callout-tip}
## New to Git and GitHub?

If you have not used Git and GitHub before, take these two free courses from GitHub first. Each takes less than an hour, and together they cover everything this setup uses: copying a repository, cloning it, and committing and pushing your changes.

- [Introduction to GitHub](https://github.com/skills/introduction-to-github): repositories, branches and commits on GitHub.
- [Introduction to Git](https://github.com/skills/introduction-to-git): Git on your own computer, in the terminal and in VS Code.
:::

## 1. Create a GitHub account

Sign up at [github.com](https://github.com/signup). The free plan is all you need.

## 2. Install Git

Download Git from [git-scm.com](https://git-scm.com/downloads) and install it. On macOS, Git is often already there. Check it in a terminal (on Windows: PowerShell):

```bash
git --version
```

Then tell Git your name and the email address of your GitHub account. Git adds them to every change you save:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

## 3. Install uv

macOS and Linux:

```bash
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
```

Close and reopen your terminal, then check that it works:

```bash
uv --version
```

Other ways to install uv are in the [uv documentation](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/).

## 4. Install VS Code

Download VS Code from [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com/) and install it.

## 5. Make your own copy of the course

1. Sign in to GitHub and open the [course repository](https://github.com/BredaUniversityADSAI/introduction-to-ml).
2. Click "Use this template" (top right), then "Create a new repository".
3. Name your repository, for example `introduction-to-ml`, and choose "Private".
4. Click "Create repository".

Your copy is now at `github.com/<your-username>/introduction-to-ml`.

## 6. Download your copy

In VS Code:

1. Open the Command Palette ("View" > "Command Palette…"), type `Git: Clone` and press Enter.
2. Choose "Clone from GitHub". The first time, VS Code asks you to sign in to GitHub in your browser. Then choose your repository from the list.
3. Choose the folder where you keep your projects. VS Code downloads your repository into a new folder there and asks whether to open it: open it.
4. VS Code offers to install the extensions the course recommends: Python and Jupyter, which run the notebooks, and Quarto (optional). Install them.

In the Explorer on the left you see the course as folders, one per Self-study theme and one per DataLab iteration, with the files numbered in the order you work through them.

## 7. Install Python and the packages

Open a terminal in VS Code ("Terminal" > "New Terminal"). It opens in the course folder. Then:

```bash
uv sync
```

The first time, this downloads Python 3.13 and all packages into a `.venv` folder inside the course folder. That takes a few minutes. Nothing is installed elsewhere on your computer. Check that it works:

```bash
uv run python -c "import sklearn, rdkit, xgboost, lightgbm; print('All set')"
```

If you see `All set`, the packages are ready. On macOS, if this fails with a message about `libomp`, install the OpenMP runtime with [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/) and try again:

```bash
brew install libomp
```

## 8. Check the notebooks

Open `self-study/theme-1/02_getting_started.ipynb`, click "Select Kernel" in the top right, choose the `.venv` environment and run all cells. If they run without errors, you are ready to start. See [Jupyter notebooks in VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/datascience/jupyter-notebooks) for more about working with notebooks.

In any notebook, this cell shows which Python it uses and the folder it runs in:

```python
import sys
from pathlib import Path
print(sys.executable)  # should be inside the course's .venv folder
print(Path.cwd())      # the folder of the notebook
```

The notebooks read the data with paths relative to their own folder: a DataLab notebook in `datalab/iteration-2/` reads `../../data/...`. Files you create (such as the processed CSV files) go in `data/002_processed_data/`, models in `models/`.

## Save your work

Work directly in the notebooks of your copy. At the end of each session, save your work to your repository on GitHub:

1. Open "Source Control" in the bar on the left of VS Code. It lists the files you changed.
2. Type a short message that says what you did, for example `Theme 1: classification exercises`.
3. Click "Commit". If VS Code asks whether to stage all your changes, choose "Yes".
4. Click "Sync Changes" to send your commits to GitHub.

Git ignores the files the notebooks create in `data/002_processed_data/`, `data/003_test_data/` and `models/`, so they stay on your computer only. On another computer, run the notebooks that create them again.

## What is where

| Folder | Contents |
|---|---|
| `self-study/` | Self-study, one folder per theme: the notebooks and the reading pages you see on this website |
| `datalab/` | DataLab, one folder per iteration: the notebooks and the pages you see on this website |
| `data/` | All datasets of the project (see `data/README.md`) |
| `models/` | Models you save while working through the notebooks |
| `tools/` | The scorer for your test-set predictions (`score.py`) |

In each theme and iteration folder, the files are numbered in the order of this website, starting with the overview page `00_overview.qmd`. Follow the [course route](course-guide.qmd#the-course-route): it takes you through Self-study and DataLab in turn. The `.qmd` files are the pages of this website: read them here, where the figures, videos and interactive parts work. The notebooks (`.ipynb`) are the files you open and run.

## Updates {#updates}

Your copy keeps the course version you started with; its number is the `version` in `pyproject.toml`. We recommend that you finish the course with this version: your notebooks already contain your work, and the course stays the same while you work through it.

This website always shows the latest version. If a page and your notebook differ, [What's new](whats-new.qmd) says what changed. If a later version fixes something you need, such as a mistake in a notebook, open the file in the [course repository](https://github.com/BredaUniversityADSAI/introduction-to-ml) and copy the part you need into your own notebook.

## Without a GitHub account

You can also download the course without a GitHub account. Follow steps 2 to 4, then download the course in a terminal, in the folder where you keep your projects, and continue with step 7:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/BredaUniversityADSAI/introduction-to-ml.git
```

You can't save your work to GitHub this way, so make your own backups. You can get a later version of the course with `git pull` and `uv sync`, but `git pull` refuses to overwrite notebooks you have changed. To avoid that, work in a copy of each notebook (for example `04_regression_mine.ipynb`) and keep the originals untouched.

## If something goes wrong

- **`uv` or `git`: command not found.** Close and reopen the terminal after installing. On Windows, use PowerShell.
- **VS Code doesn't offer "Clone from GitHub", or says Git is not installed.** Install Git (step 2) and restart VS Code.
- **VS Code asks you to configure `user.name` and `user.email`.** Run the two `git config` commands of step 2 and commit again.
- **A package is missing or behaves strangely.** Delete the `.venv` folder and run `uv sync` again.
- **`ModuleNotFoundError` in a notebook, although the check above printed `All set`.** The notebook runs in another Python. Click the kernel name in the top right of the notebook and choose the `.venv` environment.
- **`FileNotFoundError` for a data file.** Print `Path.cwd()` (see step 8) and check the path relative to that folder. If the missing file is `HOPV_homolumo_processed.csv` or `xy_df_hopv.csv`, an earlier notebook hasn't saved it yet: each Iteration 2 and 3 notebook says at the top which files it needs and which notebook creates them.
- **You want an extra package.** Run `uv add <package-name>` in the course folder and restart the notebook kernel. Don't use `pip install` inside a notebook: the package is lost at the next `uv sync`. `uv add` changes `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock`: commit them with your work.
- **Do not upgrade `rdkit`.** It is pinned to version 2025.9.3 on purpose: other versions compute some molecular descriptors differently from the course data.
- Still stuck? Ask in the course [Discussions](https://github.com/BredaUniversityADSAI/introduction-to-ml/discussions/categories/q-a). Say which operating system you use and paste the full error message.

## Only a quick look? Google Colab

Every notebook page on this website has an "Open in Colab" button. Colab runs the notebook in your browser, without installing anything, and the notebooks show how to load the data there. It is fine for a quick look or a single notebook. For the whole course, use the local setup: Colab forgets the files you create when the session ends, and the DataLab notebooks depend on files from earlier notebooks. If you still continue a DataLab notebook chain in Colab, download the files a notebook creates before the session ends, and upload them at the start of the next one.
